# Getting ready {#sec-m0-preparacao}

This is a preparatory session, to be done before the first meeting of Module 1. The
goal is simple: install what is missing and create the accounts you need **before** class, so
that class time is spent on R, not on installation.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Quick checklist

1. R and RStudio installed (@sec-m1-ambiente).
2. Module 1 data downloaded: the `dados_modulo1.zip` file from the
   [Releases](https://github.com/Joaobazzo/curso-r-transportes/releases) page, unzipped inside
   the course project folder.
3. GitHub account created, Git installed.
4. Decided which editor you will use (RStudio is the course default; see the alternatives
   below if you are curious).
5. Aware of the golden rule about AI: **do not paste data you would not publish**.
:::

## How to ask for help {#como-pedir-ajuda}

Keep this guide at hand even before you start Module 1: it applies to any question in the
course, technical or not.

1. **Repository issues**:
   <https://github.com/Joaobazzo/curso-r-transportes/issues>. Preferred: the answer stays
   on record and helps the other participants. When you open one, include the code you ran, the
   full error message and the output of `sessionInfo()`.
2. **E-mail**: for questions specific to your work that involve non-public data.
3. **In the sessions**: the first 15 minutes of each class are set aside for questions about the
   previous material.

## R and RStudio

Installing R, RStudio, Rtools (Windows) and the Module 1 packages is described in detail in
@sec-m1-ambiente. Do it now, and check in the console:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
R.version.string
#> [1] "R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24 ucrt)"
```
:::


## Editors other than RStudio

RStudio is the editor this course uses in screenshots and examples, and it is the best
choice for people starting out in R. But it is not the only option, and it is worth knowing the others
exist, especially if you also program in another language.

| Editor | What it is | When to consider it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **RStudio** | The development environment dedicated to R, by Posit. | Course default. The best choice for those who program only in R. |
| **VS Code** | Microsoft's general-purpose editor, popular across many languages. Needs the R extension and the `languageserver` package to work well with R. | People who already use VS Code for Python, SQL or another language and do not want to switch editors. |
| **Positron** | A new editor from Posit, built on the same engine as VS Code, with native support for R **and** Python in one place. | People who work with R and Python in the same project. Still maturing. |

::: {.callout-note}
## None of these choices is final

Switching editors is just switching windows: the R code is the same, the packages are the same, the
project on disk is the same. Start with RStudio, which is what this material assumes, and move
later if you feel the need.
:::

## Version control: create the account now

Git and GitHub are taught in detail in Module 4, but the two most time-consuming steps
(installing Git and creating the account) do not depend on anything in the course and are worth doing in advance:

1. Install Git: <https://git-scm.com/downloads>.
2. Create a free GitHub account: <https://github.com/>.

The rest (setting up RStudio to use Git, making the first *commit*, publishing a
repository) is left for Module 4, when there is a real project to put under version control.

## AI in development

AI assistants (GitHub Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT, and packages such as `ellmer` and `gander` inside
R) speed up R work considerably, and we come back to this topic in more detail in
@sec-m1-ambiente. The rule worth keeping from the start, because it applies to any tool:

::: {.callout-important}
## The golden rule

**If you would not publish the content on the Ministry's website, do not paste it into an AI
assistant hosted outside the organisation.** This includes personal data, exports of a contracted model,
spreadsheets from an ongoing study and any password or *token*.
:::

## R compared with other tools

A common question from people coming from spreadsheets or point-and-click GIS: why swap a
tool that already works for one that requires writing code?

| Tool | Where R helps |
|:--|:--|
| Excel / spreadsheets | A spreadsheet does not audit itself: a wrong click in a formula leaves no trace. Code does, and it runs again on its own when the data are updated. |
| QGIS / ArcGIS (menus and clicks) | The same libraries underneath (GDAL, GEOS, PROJ) — @sec-m2-sf. The difference is that the sequence of clicks is not recorded; the script is. |
| Python | Comparable in capability for this kind of analysis. The choice here is the ecosystem: `sf`, `geobr`, `r5r`, `aopdata` and the other packages in this course are specific to R and to the Brazilian context. |
| Stata / SPSS | Strong in classical statistics. R covers the same ground and, on top of that, has the spatial and Brazilian public-data ecosystem this course uses. |

None of these tools goes away: the course's aim is to reduce manual rework where it
weighs most, not to replace everything with code.
